Patient demographics:
  age: 29
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Salesperson
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Feeling Vulnerable: Feeling emotionally vulnerable, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people

Vignette:
Ethan, a 34-year-old sales representative, was driving northwest on Route 9 toward a client meeting when the sky turned the color of bruised fruit. It had rained for three days, but no one had warned him about the creek that ran beneath that stretch of road. The water came from nowhere—a wall of brown that lifted his sedan off the asphalt and spun it sideways. He remembers the sound of gravel against the undercarriage, the steering wheel wrenching out of his hands, and then nothing. The next thing he knew, he was standing waist-deep in floodwater on the shoulder of the road, gasping, his briefcase gone, his phone dead. He could not account for the missing minutes between the car spinning and his feet on solid ground. Those minutes never came back. What did come back, without warning and without image, was the feeling of being crushed, of not being able to breathe, of having no ground beneath him—and that feeling could arrive anywhere, any time, for no reason he could name.

In the weeks that followed, Ethan stopped driving Route 9. Then he stopped driving any road that ran beside a creek or a drainage ditch. He told himself it was sensible: why take the chance? But it was not only roads. He began to avoid any landscape that reminded him of that day—wooded areas, riverbanks, even the park near his apartment. The smell of wet earth after a rain would send his heart racing, his palms slick, his body braced for impact. He woke frequently during the night, sometimes several times, each time scanning the dark bedroom for something—he did not know what—and only returning to sleep after he had checked the window, the door, the floor for water. What surprised him most was how vulnerable he felt in situations that had never bothered him before—a colleague offering to drive him to lunch, a stranger asking him for directions, even a friendly tap on the shoulder. In those moments, his chest would tighten and his mind would go to the flood: the helplessness, the certainty that he was about to die alone. He had come to believe that showing any need for help was dangerous, that relying on someone else meant placing his life in hands that could not be trusted.

At work, his sales territory shrank. He declined assignments that required driving through rural or flood-prone counties. He made excuses about his car, about his schedule. His manager started to notice that Ethan was no longer the first to volunteer for the high-stakes calls. Ethan noticed too. He noticed that the part of him that used to enjoy the challenge of a cold lead, the rush of a closed deal, had vanished. He felt hollow. Nothing felt meaningful anymore—not the commissions, not the rapport he built with clients, not the weekends he spent alone in his apartment because he had stopped returning his friends’ texts. He had become certain that he could not rely on other people, that no one would have helped him if he had drowned, that the people he once called friends were too busy or too distant to matter. He had no evidence for this, but he felt it like a fact. Every time a friend reached out, he felt a wave of panic: that opening up would expose his weakness, that he would be let down again. So he stayed silent, and the silence grew.

The worst moments came when the memory hit him with its full emotional force—the terror of drowning, the certainty of death—but without any clear image attached. He would be standing in the grocery store, reaching for a can of soup, and suddenly his chest would lock and he would feel exactly what he felt in that flood, except he could not see it, could not place it. His mind would go blank, and his body would scream. During one such episode at a gas station, he found himself on the concrete, his hands over his head, a stranger asking if he needed an ambulance. He said no and drove home without buying anything. That night, lying awake at 2 a.m., he realized that the smallest triggers—feeling emotionally exposed during a phone call, feeling physically weak after a cold, even the vulnerability of being tired—could send him spiraling. He had become terrified of his own fragility, and he monitored every interaction for signs that he might feel unsafe.

By the time he walked into the clinic, Ethan had been living like this for almost eight months. His boss had told him that if he did not start covering his full territory, they would have to let him go. That ultimatum had cracked something open. He sat in the intake chair with his hands on his knees, unable to look at the therapist directly, and said that he did not know who he was anymore. He wanted to stop feeling like he was drowning on dry land. He wanted to remember what mattered. He was afraid that nothing ever would again—and afraid, too, that admitting how vulnerable he felt would only prove that he was already lost.
